Experimental method and results The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of each specimen was measured with a digital spinner magnetom- eter. At each site two specimens from different cores were subjected to demagnetization in alternating freIds in steps of 50 m lWOe (5 or I0 mT') up to 800 0e (80 mT), to test for stability. In general, small changes in remanence direction were observed after each step. Four specimens per site were demagnetized in detail by heating, which was found to be more effective in removing viscous components oriented roughly in the present local field direction. A stable end point was reached in about 70% of the specimens (Figs. 3,5,6,8). The rest of the specimens from each site were heated in three or four steps in a selected temperature interval (normally 540-670°C) on the basis of the more detailed results obtained for the four pilot specimens. Table 1 shows that this treatment resulted in substantial improve- ments in the site grouping statistics, the best grouping being shown and used in the calculation of the paleopole position. Thermal demagnetization of the trough redbeds yielded 52 core directions, each of which showed good specimen end points and sufficient homogeneity of magnetization, and 101 such core directions were obtained for the outlier redbeds. In most of these samples, there are no indications that the stable remanence is multi-component, and the fold test yields (for LC-4 Sakami Formation and the Chakonipau Formation) a significant (95% probability) improvement of the dispersion parameter K. Thus, the Chakonipau Formation remanence is probably pre-Hudsonian and the Sakami Formation remanence is probably pre-faulting (not dated). Furthermore, a near reversal (165") in the Chakonipau Formation suggests that the stable remanence was acquired during or soon after deposition. Thermal demagnetization of the trough redbeds yielded 52 core directions, each of which showed good specimen end points and sufficient homogeneity of magnetization, and 101 such core directions were obtained for the outlier redbeds. In most of these samples, there are no indications that the stable remanence is multi-component, and the fold test yields (for LC-4 Sakami Formation and the Chakonipau Formation) a significant (95% probability) improvement of the dispersion parameter K. Thus, the Chakonipau Formation remanence is probably pre-Hudsonian and the Sakami Formation remanence is probably pre-faulting (not dated). Furthermore, a near reversal (165") in the Chakonipau Formation suggests that the stable remanence was acquired during or soon after deposition. The pole positions for Circum-Superior orogen rocks, the Proterozoic outliers, and the Sutton Lake inlier suggest: (1) a time-stratigraphic correlation between the LC-4 Sakami, Dieter Lake, Sutton Lake, and the upper part of the Belcher Island sequences; and (2) a time-stratigraphic correlation between the lower part of the Belcher Islands sequence and the Richmond Gulf sequence, which m

Redbeds are known to generally possess high stability of remanent magnetization, owing to the presence of hematite, which has made them of great interest for paleomagnetic studies. On the other hand, they are known to be amenable to the addition of stable secondary remanence components because of (re)crystal- lization of hematite during diagenesis and later meta- morphism. Conclusion A Proterozoic age for the WB characteristic remanence is indicated by a straightfomard interpretation of hybrid NRM's in the gabbro and its contact rocks. WB has lower TB's and coercivities than the Kenoran component of NRM; it is therefore likely a younger overprint. It can also be argued that in view of the profound effect of the Kenoran Orogeny elsewhere in the Geotraverse region, it would be unusual if pre-Kenoran magnetizations were to have escaped Kenoran overprinting in all but a very few Wabigoon samples. The evidence against a Proterozoic regional remagnetiza- tion is fairly compelling, however. There is no indica- tion of a -1300 Ma tectonic or heating event in the region. The reversal record of the Wabigoon body implies a chilled margin and slowly cooled interior. A contact test, which would have settled the question, failed because the unbaked country rocks are either unstably magnetized or totally reset by the Kenoran Orogeny . On the basis of this evidence, it is tentatively concluded that the Wabigoon gabbro was intruded into already folded greenstones in late Archean time and has retained a characteristic remanence that largely escaped remagnetization in the Kenoran event. There is no evidence for a heating event at a later time to reset the magnetization, but rather for a very long, slow cooling history from the time of intrusion. The likely explanation for the A and C magnetizations and for the host magnetization is that they represent a time at which the magnetizations in both rock units became stabilized. Thus they would not represent reset magnetizations or primary magnetiza- tions but rather the first magnetizations retained by the respective rocks. Up to this time the mineral systems would be continually evolving and re-equilibrating until the temperature and chemical conditions were condu- cive to the retention of a stable magnetization. It is likely under these conditions that A and C were produced as TCRM's at much lower temperatures than indicated by the TUB'S. Components B and D would have been acquired later at a lower temperature. The trend in B has been explained as an effect due to the magnetic influence of A. But whether this influence could account for all the scatter in B is unknown. The effect may be partly due to resetting of magnetizations at different times, depending on the chemical conditions at a site. This seems reasonable in view of the evidence that A and C are likely TCRM's produced under similar slow cooling conditions. The recovery of pre-Grenville magnetizations would constrain future plate tectonic models of the Grenville Province. Paleomagnetic studies have generally been confined to the easily accessible southwestern portion of the Grenville Province, where a high grade of metamor- phism prevails. Two areas, the Hastings Lowlands of southeastern Ontario, and the northeastern part of the Grenville Province in Labrador, have significantly lower grades of metamorphism, and thus provide better opportunities for recovering primary magnetizations (Dunlop et al. 1980). In the Hastings Lowlands, paleomagnetic studies of the Thanet gabbros have offered equivocal evidence of the presence of primary magnetization (Buchan 1978; Dunlop et al. 1980). Previous studies in Labrador on units along the Gren- ville Front (Fahrig and Larochelle 1972; Fahrig et al. 1974) have also yielded somewhat equivocal results, possibly due to inadequate analysis. The present paleo- magnetic study from the Mealy dykes of Labrador, located well south of the Grenville Front, provided a good opportunity for recovering a primary magnetiza- tion. The recovery of pre-Grenville magnetizations would constrain future plate tectonic models of the Grenville Province. Paleomagnetic studies have generally been confined to the easily accessible southwestern portion of the Grenville Province, where a high grade of metamor- phism prevails. Two areas, the Hastings Lowlands of southeastern Ontario, and the northeastern part of the Grenville Province in Labrador, have significantly lower grades of metamorphism, and thus provide better opportunities for recovering primary magnetizations (Dunlop et al. 1980). In the Hastings Lowlands, paleomagnetic studies of the Thanet gabbros have offered equivocal evidence of the presence of primary magnetization (Buchan 1978; Dunlop et al. 1980). Previous studies in Labrador on units along the Gren- ville Front (Fahrig and Larochelle 1972; Fahrig et al. 1974) have also yielded somewhat equivocal results, possibly due to inadequate analysis. The present paleo- magnetic study from the Mealy dykes of Labrador, located well south of the Grenville Front, provided a good opportunity for recovering a primary magnetiza- tion. Avalonian microcontinent using the stable remanence of Ordovician oolitic hematite ores may have yielded a Devonian paleopole since the ores may never have been deeply buried but were in a region of Devonian low-grade metamorphism. Although oolitic hematite is not nor- mally present in continental red beds, other colloform hema- tites have been reported (Turner and Ixer 1977); these may also have dehydrated from goethite at -80°C, adding to the com- plexity of remanence often reported (Turner 1980) in con- tinental red beds. Our results emphasize that the paleo- magnetism of red beds should be interpreted with caution. A positive fold test is not necessarily evidence of primary rem- anence and burial history may control the timing of remanence acquisition through diagenetic chemical changes. A test of whether oolitic hematites have commonly trans- formed from goethites at -80°C may be possible by estimating the maximum temperature experienced by many oolitic hema- tites and goethites using indicators such as conodont colour and vitrinite reflectance. If the test is positive, paleomagnetism may allow dating of when oolitic hematites were first heated to -80°C, perhaps aiding studies of the history of heating and oil maturation in sedimentary basins. In the earlier paper I suggested that one of the resolved magnetizations (called B), thought to be carried by hematite pigment, was prefolding, and nearly coeval with the primary remanence. But evidence from a fold test was equivocal. The main purpose in publishing the present results is to prove that B is prefolding (pre-Paleocene at latest), and thus provide a time constraint for the acquisition of the pigment. The present results were mainly obtained from the acid leaching of sandstones. The chemical leaching technique gen- erally allows the direction of the removed pigment to be deter- mined by vector subtraction or vector diagrams. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: separated Methods Hand samples, collected in the field, were oriented by sun and magnetic compasses. Samples were cored in the lab- oratory; cores were cut into as many as five standard specimens (2.2 cm in height). After measurement of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM), specimens were subjected to alternating field (AF) treatment, thermal demagnetization, or acid leaching, in steps. Later, the acid-leached specimens were AF or thermally de- magnetized. AF and thermal treatments were conducted on apparatus described by Roy et al. (1969, 1972, 1973) in ambi- ent fields generally less than 2 nT. Acid leaching or chemical demagnetization was carried out using the general procedures of Park (1970). Thus, after axial holes had been drilled through specimens to facilitate leaching, specimens were leached in HCl (6- 10 N), washed in water, dried, and measured. Leaching was discontinued when re- manent magnetizations ceased to change with further treatment (after about 2000-7600 h in acid). To remove any viscous remanent magnetization (VRM) ac- quired during leaching, several procedures were used. [Traduit par le journal] Can. J. Earth Sci. 21, 544-553 (1984) Geology The Tulemalu dykes make up a fairly widespread swarm centred on the Tulemalu map area of southern Keewatin. They extend into, but are less abundant in, the northern half of the Ferguson Lake map area to the east (Fig. I), and a few dykes of similar character have been reported both to the north and south of the Tulemalu Lake map area (Eade 1984). The pre- dominant trend of the Tulemalu dykes is easterly to east- southeasterly, and radioisotopic dating and field relationships indicate that they are early Aphebian (see Eade and Wanless in Wanless et al. 1980). Eade (1984) has indicated that some easterly trending members of the swarm were emplaced in fault zones and

hebian (see Eade and Wanless in Wanless et al. 1980). Eade (1984) has indicated that some easterly trending members of the swarm were emplaced in fault zones and that later movement on the faults has imparted in- tense cleavage to some of these dykes. Most of the dykes, however, do not have trends that parallel the known regional faults so they probably reflect a tensional regime differing from that existing during the formation of the fault systems. The Tulemalu dykes are not identifiable on standard Geolog- ical Survey of Canada 1 : 50 000 aeromagnetic maps so most of the dykes shown in Fig. 2 were identified by direct ground or air observation. Dykes do seem to be apparent on more detailed aeromagnetic maps, and the pattern within the rectangle out- lined by dots in Fig. 2 was derived from 1 : 20 000 maps loaned by Pan Ocean Oil Limited. Linear anomalies on these maps agree well with dykes as mapped on the ground so it is very likely that they indicate the presence of dykes. Metamorphic alteration of silicate minerals in Tulemalu ma- terial from sites sampled for paleomagnetic study varies from extremely slight to moderate. This is not surprising because hornblende can be very resistant to argon loss in response to short-lived thermal events of this type. The dykes with which these hornblendes were in contact were only 16 m thick. The other two contact hornblendes yielded ages of 2250 Ma. [Traduit par le journal] Can. J. Earth Sci. 21, 544-553 (1984) Geology The Tulemalu dykes make up a fairly widespread swarm centred on the Tulemalu map area of southern Keewatin. They extend into, but are less abundant in, the northern half of the Ferguson Lake map area to the east (Fig. I), and a few dykes of similar character have been reported both to the north and south of the Tulemalu Lake map area (Eade 1984). The pre- dominant trend of the Tulemalu dykes is easterly to east- southeasterly, and radioisotopic dating and field relationships indicate that they are early Aphebian (see Eade and Wanless in Wanless et al. 1980). Eade (1984) has indicated that some easterly trending members of the swarm were emplaced in fault zones and

hebian (see Eade and Wanless in Wanless et al. 1980). Eade (1984) has indicated that some easterly trending members of the swarm were emplaced in fault zones and that later movement on the faults has imparted in- tense cleavage to some of these dykes. Most of the dykes, however, do not have trends that parallel the known regional faults so they probably reflect a tensional regime differing from that existing during the formation of the fault systems. The Tulemalu dykes are not identifiable on standard Geolog- ical Survey of Canada 1 : 50 000 aeromagnetic maps so most of the dykes shown in Fig. 2 were identified by direct ground or air observation. Dykes do seem to be apparent on more detailed aeromagnetic maps, and the pattern within the rectangle out- lined by dots in Fig. 2 was derived from 1 : 20 000 maps loaned by Pan Ocean Oil Limited. Linear anomalies on these maps agree well with dykes as mapped on the ground so it is very likely that they indicate the presence of dykes. Metamorphic alteration of silicate minerals in Tulemalu ma- terial from sites sampled for paleomagnetic study varies from extremely slight to moderate. The alteration takes the form of slight chloritization of mafic minerals in least altered dykes to development of amphibole coronas aroun

This is not surprising because hornblende can be very resistant to argon loss in response to short-lived thermal events of this type. The dykes with which these hornblendes were in contact were only 16 m thick. The other two contact hornblendes yielded ages of 2250 Ma. he samples are unusually magnetic for granites, with natural re- manent magnetizations (NRM's) generally < 2 X emu cm-3 (2 A m-I), there was no difficulty in orienting samples using a magnetic compass. No contact test was attempted, since the only accessible contact with Couchiching series schists to the southeast forms the channel of the Maligne River. In the laboratory, three or four 2.5 cm specimens were drilled from each block. A full program of measurements was carried out on every sample. One specimen was thermally demagnetized, usually in 50°C steps to 500°C and then in 25°C steps to 675"C, using a noninductive furnace in a three-axis Helmholtz-coil array. The remaining two or three specimens were alternating field (AF) demagnetized in 12 steps to 1000 Oe (0.1 T) in a Schonstedt demagnetizer. Magnetizations were measured after each step with a Digico spinner magnetometer. Results were accepted if specimen magnetization vectors achieved a stable grouping different from the present Earth's field (PEF) at higher AF's or temperatures and if within-sample divergences were <20°. The present paper describes similar studies carried out on the Burchell Lake granite of the Shebandowan- Wawa volcanic subprovince, which lies to the east of the Quetico Subprovince. A location map is given in 11. The natural remanent magnetizations (NRM's) of the Bur- chell Lake and Shelley Lake granites have much in common. Type 1 NRM, which was argued to be the primary 2580 Ma magnetization of the Shelley Lake body, is the characteristic Burchell Lake NRM. Type 2 NRM, a late Proterozoic re- magnetization component found in about a dozen Shelley Lake samples, is identified in a few Burchell Lake samples, but is rather poorly defined, perhaps because NRM intensities tend to be an order of magnitude lower (geometric mean 45 x emu/cm3 (0.045 A/m)) than in the Shelley Lake granite (mean 300 X emu/cm3 (0.3 A/m)). The Burchell Lake pluton has not been dated radiometric- ally. Granitic bodies a few miles distant have K/Ar biotite ages in the range 2550-2610 Ma (e.g., Giblin 1964, p. 21). Earth Sci. 21, 1460-1472 (1984) Introduction An increasing number of post-Paleozoic ultramafic rocks have been described west of the Appalachian fold belt. These occurrences include: Ile Bizard, Quebec (Clark 1972; Raeside and Helmstaedt 1982), Ithaca, New York (Martens 1924; Watson 1967; Zartman et al. 1967; Kay et al. 1983), Dixonville and Masontown, Pennsylvania (Deines 19

dikes of post-Ordovician age have been rec- 'Present address: Cominco Ltd., 409 Grenville St., Vancouver, B.C., Canada V6C 2R2. ognized at two localities north of Lake Ontario (Fig. 1). One of the dikes, discovered by C. G. Winder, is exposed in a quarry near the town of Picton. The second dike, exposed near the northwest comer of Varty Lake, was examined by Hon (1970), who concluded that this dike is a micaceous kimberlite. The Picton and Varty Lake dikes are the first post-Paleozoic ultra- mafic igneous rocks reported from the stable Paleozoic plat- form of southern Ontario. This paper provides basic informa- tion concerning the petrography, mineralogy, and mineral chemistry of these two occurrences and includes an estimate of the time of emplacement resulting from the application of the K- Ar and paleomagnetic techniques. General geology Both the Picton and Varty Lake dikes intrude limestones of the Ordovician Black River and Trenton groups. The Picton dike is exposed in the limestone quarry (44"03'N, 77'08'W) of the Lake Ontario Cement Company Limited located 4 km north of Picton. Host Trenton limestones are heavily jointed in the quarry but with no apparent vertical displacement across joints. The Picton dike occurs in one such joint exposed on three A Dike loca

osed over a dis- tance of 150 m in five prospect pits near the northwest comer of Varty Lake (44"25'N, 76"49'W). In the most complete ex- posure, the dike is 1.5 m wide and is vertical, with a strike of 120". The limestone host rocks are flat lying in the area but beds have been tilted up about 15" on either side of the dike. Both dikes trend approximately normal to north-northeast- trending regional faults (Fig. I). Analytical procedures Selected inclusion-free samples were crushed and analysed by the X-ray fluorescence method for whole-rock and trace- element compositions. The mineral chemistry was examined with a mode[ 400 MAC electron microprobe and all data were processed using Magic IV matrix corrections. The K- Ar dating procedure is identical to that described by Hayatsu and Carmichael (1977). Two large samples from the Picton dike and one from Varty Lake were crushed to 20 mesh and s~iit in two. One portion was used untreated for a regular whole-rock method, and the other half was treated with 10% HCI to remove carbonate minerals before K and Ar deter- minations. A phlogopite mineral separate was also prepared from the Varty Lake dike for K-Ar determination. , 1984 The Picton and Varty Lake ultramafic dikes that intrude Ordovician limestone near Belleville, Ontario, consist of olivine or serpentinized pseudomorphs and Ti-phlogopite phenocrysts set in a groundmass of spinel, perovskite, serpentine, calcite, apatite, and chlorite. Phlogopite exhibits a complex chemical variation and late-stage Ba enrichment (up to 6.8 wt.% BaO). Spinels are chemically zoned and commonly exhibit an atoll texture in which a magnesian-aluminous chromite core is separated by a silicate zone from late-stage magnesian-aluminous titanomagnetite chemically similar to kimberlitic spinel. Atoll spinels from the Picton dike also have a zone of titanian pleonaste surrounding a central grain of magnesian-aluminous chromite at the centre of the atoll structures. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: hwest- trending Hearst dikes have a mean remanence direction rotated - 15" counterclockwise from both north-trending Hearst dikes near the southern KSZ and the north-trending Matachewan dikes (Table 1). The directions are statistically different at the 0.05 confidence level (statistics from Tarling 1983). One pos- sible explanation is that the northwest dikes have been rotated counterclockwise relative to the north dikes during deformation along the KSZ, as suggested by Bennett et al. (1967). How- ever, the declination difference (- 15") is less than the change in dike trend (25-40"), so some of the variation in dike trend must be primary. Other explanations for the paleomagnetic data are that the northwest-trending dikes are of a slightly different age, or that the remanence vector is biassed into the plane of the dike (Strangway 1961). This latter possibility needs to be checked by detailed rock magnetic studies but was not revealed in a statistical study of worldwide paleomagnetic data obtained from dikes (Evans 1968). Structural and paleomagnetic data from the Hearst dikes support the model of crustal tilting associated with KSZ thrusting proposed by Percival and Card (1983) and indicate that this deformation occurred at least in part subsequent to dike intrusion (i.e., after 2.6 Ga). Dikes on the eastern side of the KSZ comprise: (1) 2.6 Ga north-trending Matachewan quartz tholeiites, (2) 2.15 Ga northeast-trending Preissac tholeiites, and (3) 1.15 Ga east- northeast-trending Abitibi alkali olivine basalts (Fahrig 1972; Card et al. 1981; Gates and Hurley 1973; Hanes and York 1979). Although several paleomagnetic studies have been done on these dikes (e.g., Strangway 1961, 1964; Larochelle 1966; Irving and Naldrett 1977; Buchan and Schwarz 1981; Schutts and Dunlop 198 l), a clear picture of variation in primary direc- tion and polarity within any one swarm has yet to emerge. Comparatively little is known about the dikes west of the KSZ. Information is largely confined to reconnaissance petrog- raphy and petrochemistry (Siragusa 1977; Thurston et al. 1977; Card et al. 1981). K-Ar ages on NW-trending dikes range from 2.4 to 1.4 Ga (Wanless et al. 1966; W. F. Fahrig, personal communication, 1984). The individual units, including baked- contact rocks, have distinctive natural remanent magnetization (NRM) properties as a result of their rather different propor- tions of coarse- and fine-grained pyrrhotite, magnetite, and hematite. The R component has the same direction as the NRM of the 2630 Ma Matachewan diabase (Irving and Naldrett 1977), whereas the N component resembles the primary NRM of the 2580 Ma Shelley Lake granite (Dunlop 1984~). A paleomagnetic study was made to elucidate the ambiguities of the radiometric ages of Mont Megantic intrusions in relation to field observations and to determine the magnetochronology of the intruded rocks. Some 179 samples (550 specimens) were collected over 58 sites, and their magnetization was cleaned by thermal and (or) alternating field treatment. The paleopoles obtained for the Compton Formation metasediments indicate an Early to Middle Devonian age and for the overlying Frontenac Formation metavolcanics indicate an age definitely different from that for the intrusive rocks. The baked contact test on the hornfels forming the contact metamorphic aureole is positive, and the magnetization component was acquired in the Early to Late Cretaceous interval. Syenite contains two components: one with normal polarity, the other with reversed polarity; their ages are Juro-Cretaceous. The paleopoles obtained for the Compton Formation metasediments indicate an Early to Middle Devonian age and for the overlying Frontenac Formation metavolcanics indicate an age definitely different from that for the intrusive rocks. The baked contact test on the hornfels forming the contact metamorphic aureole is positive, and the magnetization component was acquired in the Early to Late Cretaceous interval. Syenite contains two components: one with normal polarity, the other with reversed polarity; their ages are Juro-Cretaceous. The gabbro contains only one magnetization component (reversed), which was acquired in the Early Cretaceous, whereas the granite bears one component with a mostly normal polarity; its intrusive age is Late Cretaceous. The paleomagnetic ages for the intrusive rocks support the multiple intrusion interpretation; it appears that the emplacement of the intrusive bodies is Juro-Late Cretaceous. The A magnetization (eight sites, 83 specimens, D = 30.3", I = 56.7", ay, = 4.9", paleolatitude = 37 t SON, paleopole 65.0°N, 14.9OW, Ay, = 6.2") is considered to have been acquired in the age range 105-90 Ma. This result differs from the field established for cratonic North America in this time range. The difference could be caused either by previously undetected tilting about a horizontal axis of the plutons, or by their rotation about a vertical axis and lateral displacement relative to the craton. Previously observed mid-Cretaceous magnetizations from other rock units from the western Canadian Cordillera and the Cascades of Washington, United States, are similarly discordant with respect to the craton. This similarity over such a large area indicat

therefore that lateral displacement and rotation have occurred. It would seem that much of the western part of the Canadian Cordillera has moved north by about 2400 km and rotated clockwise since the mid-Cretaceous. The paleolatitude of the southern Coast Plutonic Complex of British Columbia is statistically identical to that recently observed (39 * 3ON) for three plutons from the Central Sierra Nevada of California, which raises the possibility that the two complexes were much closer together at the time of their emplacement than at present. Earth Sci. 22, 553-566 (1985) Introduction The komatiitic basalts of the Ottawa Islands are thought (Baragar and PichC 1982) to be an extension of the komatiitic suite of the Cape Smith Belt of northern Quebec. At Cape Smith, the steeply dipping, northwest-facing ko- matiitic lavas are uniformly magnetized (Fujiwara and Schwarz 1975) with a remanence direction of D = 218", 1 = 60°, k = 47, a,5 = 4". Since they dip uniformly, their magnetization neither clearly pre- nor postdates folding. Farther

Some of the massive lavas are fractionated and so comprise an olivine-cumulate layer near their base and vari- ously fractionated basalts in their upper levels. More rarely the upper part of such layered flows is marked by coarse spinifex- textured pyroxene and olivine. The volcanic succession sampled for the paleomagnetic studies (Fig. 2) forms a homoclinal sequence facing northwest and ranging in dip from about 40 to 45' westerly on the eastern side of Gilmour Island to 15' on the western side. Repetition of parts of the sequence by faulting is possible, since lineaments can be seen on air photographs, but no direct evidence for this is available. Assuming an unfaulted sequence, the thickness represented in the map of Fig. 2 would be about 4500 m. The rocks are generally metamorphosed to greenschist facies but commonly contain relicts of the primary minerals in varying proportions. Deformation is slight or absent and most rocks retain their igneous texture sufficiently well that their primary mineralogy can be readily interpreted. The rocks were originally composed of olivine and clino- pyroxene mainly, with accessory chromite, magnetite, and, to a lesser degree, chalcopyrite and pyrite. Plagioclase is present in the low-Mg lavas but is not generally in excess of about 10 or 15%. Olivine typically occurred as phenocrysts composing from about 15 to about 50% of the rock and was rarely present in the groundmass. Clinopyroxene, on the other hand, was a subordinate phenocryst phase but formed the bulk of the groundmass where it generally appeared as parallel or plumose acicular crystals commonly interleaved with plagioclase or opaque-charged glass (now chlorite). Chromite most com- monly crystallized in or adjoining olivine phenocrysts. Al- though in most samples magn

astern Hudson Bay are on strike with and believed to form a continuation of similar units of the Cape Smith Belt 150 km to the northeast. Units sampled in the Ottawa Islands all dip gently to the west and hence are not suitable for an internal fold test of their age of magnetization. However, before correcting for the tilt of the lavas, the dominant magnetization direction (D = 207.6", 1 = 61.9", k = 168, a,, = 3.7") does not differ significantly from the uncorrected magnetization direction reported from the steeply dipping, northwest-facing units at Cape Smith (D = 218", I = 60°, k = 47, = 4"). This negative fold test suggests that the remanence at both locations was acquired after folding. Comparison with the North American Precambrian apparent polar wander path implies that overprinting is related to the Hudsonian Orogeny . A second stable magnetization directed to the west with a shallow inclination is superimposed on the dominant component at a number of sampling sites. Its direction is poorly defined and no fold test is possible. However, magnetic evidence suggests that this component was probably acquired as an overprint after the dominant magnetization, perhaps during a mild reheating associated with the Elsonian Orogeny. The valley was cut to a maximum depth of 150 m after the river was diverted southeastward by the last retreating Wisconsin ice lobe (Stalker 1960). Therefore the outcrop is not deeply weathered. ervals less than 2 m thick could probably not be relied upon for correlation, and as a consequence routine site spacing was increased to 1.5 m for the remainder of the succession. Using 7.5 Ma for the length of the Maastrichtian, the aver- age rate of sedimentation in this area was 1 m/30 000 - 35 000 years, and a 1.5 m site spacing thus represents roughly 50 000 years. Polarity zones documented by two sites therefore represent about 100 000 years and are probably useful for regional correlation. Magnetic measurements Alternating field (AF) demagnetization at 100-300 Oe (10-30 mT) is effective in removing VRM, but will not remove high-coercivity CRM, which would require thermal demagnetization. Because our sampling technique requires retention of the samples in plastic bottles throughout the mea- suring process, thermal demagnetization cannot be applied as a routine technique. Thus AF demagnetization was done in the expectation that it would be adequate for routine work. A two-axis tumbler similar to that described by McElhinny (1966) was used. Most of the early measurements were made on a Digico "complete results" spinner magnetometer; later ones were on an SCT three-axis cryogenic magnetometer. The detrital magnetic component will vary in grain size and therefore magnet

nesis and weathering in the different lithologies. For these reasons there is considerable variation in the strength of magnetization, and it is to be expected that different lithologies may behave differ- ently during cleaning. On the average, the sandstones have the largest NRM, with a mean of about 2.6 X emu/cm3 (kA/m). However, they also have the largest proportion of soft magnetism, often largely removed by AF cleaning at 100 Oe (10 mT) peak field, reducing the remaining magnetic moment to about half of the NRM value (median destructive field). The mudstones and shales have a mean NRM of about 1.5 X emu/cm3 but have a smaller soft component, resulting in a more gradual decrease in magnetization during cleaning and a median destructive field between 100 and 200 Oe (10 and 20 mT). Most of the soft mag- netism in these is lost at 100 Oe (10 mT), but very little at 50 Oe (5 mT). This succes- sion, approximately 350 m thick, is fluvial-deltaic, becoming more fluviatile upwards. The principal lithologies, in order of decreasing abundance, are greyish olive floodplain mudstones, light grey fine- to medium-grained channel sandstones, back- swamp carbonaceous shales and coals, grey to brown lacustrine shales, and siltstones. The sequence, named the Edmonton Group, is made up of the Horseshoe Canyon, Whitemud, Battle, and Scollard formations, from bottom to top (see Gibson 1977). This group is underlain conformably by the marine Bearpaw Shale and overlain conformably to discon- formably by the fluvial Paskapoo Formation. There are no extraformational conglomerates in the sequence, no obvious deep channel scours, and no documented stratigraphic breaks of consequence. The gabbro and tonalite, exposed in the northernmost portion of the Boston Basin, were selected for this study because of the lack of significant macroscopic evidence of penetrative metamorphism or deformation. The tonalite has not been radiometrically dated; however, an Ordovician date has been reported for the gabbro. Detailed petrographic data indicate that the five populations of paleomagnetic directions obtained for the gabbro and tonalite correspond to five styles of magnetic mineral alteration. A mean alteration index was calculated for each site in the Nahant gabbro and tonalite. There is an apparent relationship between magnetite alteration and normalized intensity at a given demagnetization level, with normalized intensity decreasing as magnetite alteration increases. This relationship illustrates the interdependence between paleomagnetic properties and magnetic minerals. Alteration of these minerals is probably associated with periods of magnetic overprinting.

This study was designed to obtain a reliable paleomagnetic pole for the Milford-Dedham zone, located in eastern Massa- chusetts east of the Bloody Bluff fault zone (Fig. 1). The Ordovician Nahant gabbro and a tonalite associated with the gabbro were selected for the study based on their apparent megascopically unmetamorphosed state and the fact that the gabbro has been radiometrically dated by Zartman and Marvin (1971). Schutts et al. (1976) reported a paleomagnetic pole on a Precambrian mafic complex northwest of Boston. This pole was interpreted as Devonian based on biotite-amphibole K- Ar blocking temperatures. Hurley and Shearer (1981) pub- lished a paleomagnetic pole on the Proterozoic Z Salem gabbro-diorite, which was also interpreted as Devonian based on the results of Schutts et al. (1976). Geology and age The Nahant gabbro crops out mainly along the coast of Nahant, approximately 14 km northeast of Boston. The gabbro is intruded into a northeast-southwest-trending syncline in the Lower Cambrian Weymouth Formation. Diorites and tonalites are associated with the gabbro (Fig. 2). Verma (1973) reported veins of the diorite intruding the gabbro on an island off the northeast coast of Nahant. Because no noticeable change in grain size

, some dikes may be as old as Precambrian. Laboratory procedures Nine sites were sampled at Nahant, seven in the main gabbro (1 - 3, 5, 7-9), one in the tonalite (6), and one in a diabase dike (4) that intrudes the gabbro (Fig. 2). A total of 62 samples were obtained. Results from the gabbro and tonalite only are presented in this paper. Paleomagnetic measurements were performed on a Molspin Minspin magnetometer. Stepwise demagnetization was per- formed on all but one specimen per site using a Schonstedt alternating field (AF) specimen demagnetizer in fields up to 100 mT. The remaining samples were demagnetized using a Schonstedt thermal demagnetization furnace. Three 2.5 cm diameter polished sections per site were examined using high power (X400-1000) oil-immersion reflected-light microscopy. Properties such as crystal form, grain size, primary intergrowths, and alteration products were noted for each polished section. Volume percents of the opaque minerals were estimated by point counting an average of 250 grains per section. Thin sections representative of the Nahant gabbro and tonalite were also examined for evidence of silicate metamorphism. This study was designed to obtain a reliable paleomagnetic pole for the Milford-Dedham zone, located in eastern Massa- chusetts east of the Bloody Bluff fault zone (Fig. 1). The Ordovician Nahant gabbro and a tonalite associated with the gabbro were selected for the study based on their apparent megascopically unmetamorphosed state and the fact that the gabbro has been radiometrically dated by Zartman and Marvin (1971). Schutts et al. (1976) reported a paleomagnetic pole on a Precambrian mafic complex northwest of Boston. This pole was interpreted as Devonian based on biotite-amphibole K- Ar blocking temperatures. Hurley and Shearer (1981) pub- lished a paleomagnetic pole on the Proterozoic Z Salem gabbro-diorite, which was also interpreted as Devonian based on the results of Schutts et al. (1976). Geology and age The Nahant gabbro crops out mainly along the coast of Nahant, approximately 14 km northeast of Boston. The gabbro is intruded into a northeast-southwest-trending syncline in the Lower Cambrian Weymouth Formation. Diorites and tonalites are associated with the gabbro (Fig. 2). Verma (1973) reported veins of the diorite intruding the gabbro on an island off the northeast coast of Nahant. Because no noticeable change in grain size

, some dikes may be as old as Precambrian. Laboratory procedures Nine sites were sampled at Nahant, seven in the main gabbro (1 - 3, 5, 7-9), one in the tonalite (6), and one in a diabase dike (4) that intrudes the gabbro (Fig. 2). A total of 62 samples were obtained. Results from the gabbro and tonalite only are presented in this paper. Paleomagnetic measurements were performed on a Molspin Minspin magnetometer. Stepwise demagnetization was per- formed on all but one specimen per site using a Schonstedt alternating field (AF) specimen demagnetizer in fields up to 100 mT. The remaining samples were demagnetized using a Schonstedt thermal demagnetization furnace. Three 2.5 cm diameter polished sections per site were examined using high power (X400-1000) oil-immersion reflected-light microscopy. Properties such as crystal form, grain size, primary intergrowths, and alteration products were noted for each polished section. Volume percents of the opaque minerals were estimated by point counting an average of 250 grains per section. Thin sections representative of the Nahant gabbro and tonalite were also examined for evidence of silicate metamorphism. The gabbro and tonalite poles are similar to a number of poles from Ordovician to Devonian intrusives in the Acadia terrane, including the St. Stephen and St. George plutons. This study was designed to obtain a reliable paleomagnetic pole for the Milford-Dedham zone, located in eastern Massa- chusetts east of the Bloody Bluff fault zone (Fig. 1). The Ordovician Nahant gabbro and a tonalite associated with the gabbro were selected for the study based on their apparent megascopically unmetamorphosed state and the fact that the gabbro has been radiometrically dated by Zartman and Marvin (1971). Schutts et al. (1976) reported a paleomagnetic pole on a Precambrian mafic complex northwest of Boston. This pole was interpreted as Devonian based on biotite-amphibole K- Ar blocking temperatures. Hurley and Shearer (1981) pub- lished a paleomagnetic pole on the Proterozoic Z Salem gabbro-diorite, which was also interpreted as Devonian based on the results of Schutts et al. (1976). Geology and age The Nahant gabbro crops out mainly along the coast of Nahant, approximately 14 km northeast of Boston. The gabbro is intruded into a northeast-southwest-trending syncline in the Lower Cambrian Weymouth Formation. Diorites and tonalites are associated with the gabbro (Fig. 2). Verma (1973) reported veins of the diorite intruding the gabbro on an island off the northeast coast of Nahant. Because no noticeable change in grain size

, some dikes may be as old as Precambrian. Laboratory procedures Nine sites were sampled at Nahant, seven in the main gabbro (1 - 3, 5, 7-9), one in the tonalite (6), and one in a diabase dike (4) that intrudes the gabbro (Fig. 2). A total of 62 samples were obtained. Results from the gabbro and tonalite only are presented in this paper. Paleomagnetic measurements were performed on a Molspin Minspin magnetometer. Stepwise demagnetization was per- formed on all but one specimen per site using a Schonstedt alternating field (AF) specimen demagnetizer in fields up to 100 mT. The remaining samples were demagnetized using a Schonstedt thermal demagnetization furnace. Three 2.5 cm diameter polished sections per site were examined using high power (X400-1000) oil-immersion reflected-light microscopy. Properties such as crystal form, grain size, primary intergrowths, and alteration products were noted for each polished section. Volume percents of the opaque minerals were estimated by point counting an average of 250 grains per section. Thin sections representative of the Nahant gabbro and tonalite were also examined for evidence of silicate metamorphism. The gabbro and tonalite, exposed in the northernmost portion of the Boston Basin, were selected for this study because of the lack of significant macroscopic evidence of penetrative metamorphism or deformation. The tonalite has not been radiometrically dated; however, an Ordovician date has been reported for the gabbro. Detailed petrographic data indicate that the five populations of paleomagnetic directions obtained for the gabbro and tonalite correspond to five styles of magnetic mineral alteration. A mean alteration index was calculated for each site in the Nahant gabbro and tonalite. There is an apparent relationship between magnetite alteration and normalized intensity at a given demagnetization level, with normalized intensity decreasing as magnetite alteration increases. This relationship illustrates the interdependence between paleomagnetic properties and magnetic minerals. Alteration of these minerals is probably associated with periods of magnetic overprinting.

Whether the metasomatism was deuteric or the result of postdeuteric hydrothermal activity has not been determined. The Nahant gabbro poles are interpreted as representing either a deuteric or a metasomatic chemical remanent magnetization (CRM). The tonalite pole is interpreted as a deuteric CRM. The gabbro and tonalite poles are similar to a number of poles from Ordovician to Devonian intrusives in the Acadia terrane, including the St. Stephen and St. George plutons. Petrographic examination of polished sections from the Devonian St. Stephen and St. George plutons reveals evidence for alteration of primary magnetic mineral assemblages. Similarities exist between these alterations and alterations observed in the Nahant suite, most notably, the formation of titanite from Fe-Ti oxides. This study was designed to obtain a reliable paleomagnetic pole for the Milford-Dedham zone, located in eastern Massa- chusetts east of the Bloody Bluff fault zone (Fig. 1). The Ordovician Nahant gabbro and a tonalite associated with the gabbro were selected for the study based on their apparent megascopically unmetamorphosed state and the fact that the gabbro has been radiometrically dated by Zartman and Marvin (1971). Schutts et al. (1976) reported a paleomagnetic pole on a Precambrian mafic complex northwest of Boston. This pole was interpreted as Devonian based on biotite-amphibole K- Ar blocking temperatures. Hurley and Shearer (1981) pub- lished a paleomagnetic pole on the Proterozoic Z Salem gabbro-diorite, which was also interpreted as Devonian based on the results of Schutts et al. (1976). Geology and age The Nahant gabbro crops out mainly along the coast of Nahant, approximately 14 km northeast of Boston. The gabbro is intruded into a northeast-southwest-trending syncline in the Lower Cambrian Weymouth Formation. Diorites and tonalites are associated with the gabbro (Fig. 2). Verma (1973) reported veins of the diorite intruding the gabbro on an island off the northeast coast of Nahant. Because no noticeable change in grain size

, some dikes may be as old as Precambrian. Laboratory procedures Nine sites were sampled at Nahant, seven in the main gabbro (1 - 3, 5, 7-9), one in the tonalite (6), and one in a diabase dike (4) that intrudes the gabbro (Fig. 2). A total of 62 samples were obtained. Results from the gabbro and tonalite only are presented in this paper. Paleomagnetic measurements were performed on a Molspin Minspin magnetometer. Stepwise demagnetization was per- formed on all but one specimen per site using a Schonstedt alternating field (AF) specimen demagnetizer in fields up to 100 mT. The remaining samples were demagnetized using a Schonstedt thermal demagnetization furnace. Three 2.5 cm diameter polished sections per site were examined using high power (X400-1000) oil-immersion reflected-light microscopy. Properties such as crystal form, grain size, primary intergrowths, and alteration products were noted for each polished section. Volume percents of the opaque minerals were estimated by point counting an average of 250 grains per section. Thin sections representative of the Nahant gabbro and tonalite were also examined for evidence of silicate metamorphism. Verma (1973) reported veins of the diorite intruding the gabbro on an island off the northeast coast of Nahant. Because no noticeable change in grain size was observed towards the contact, the diorite was not considered a separate intrusion but rather as evidence for mul- tiple intrusive episodes of a single, larger magmatic event. The gabbro is a medium-grained, subhedral to subophitic, greenish gray to dark gray rock containing labradorite and augite, with minor hypersthene, biotite, magnetite, and ilmenite. Epidote I has been reported on slickensided fault surfaces (Kaye 1965). Verma (1973) reported evidence for low-grade metamorphism 1 of the gabbro, particularly in the vicinity of small faults. This study was designed to obtain a reliable paleomagnetic pole for the Milford-Dedham zone, located in eastern Massa- chusetts east of the Bloody Bluff fault zone (Fig. 1). The Ordovician Nahant gabbro and a tonalite associated with the gabbro were selected for the study based on their apparent megascopically unmetamorphosed state and the fact that the gabbro has been radiometrically dated by Zartman and Marvin (1971). Schutts et al. (1976) reported a paleomagnetic pole on a Precambrian mafic complex northwest of Boston. This pole was interpreted as Devonian based on biotite-amphibole K- Ar blocking temperatures. Hurley and Shearer (1981) pub- lished a paleomagnetic pole on the Proterozoic Z Salem gabbro-diorite, which was also interpreted as Devonian based on the results of Schutts et al. (1976). Geology and age The Nahant gabbro crops out mainly along the coast of Nahant, approximately 14 km northeast of Boston. The gabbro is intruded into a northeast-southwest-trending syncline in the Lower Cambrian Weymouth Formation. Diorites and tonalites are associated with the gabbro (Fig. 2). Verma (1973) reported veins of the diorite intruding the gabbro on an island off the northeast coast of Nahant. Because no noticeable change in grain size

, some dikes may be as old as Precambrian. Laboratory procedures Nine sites were sampled at Nahant, seven in the main gabbro (1 - 3, 5, 7-9), one in the tonalite (6), and one in a diabase dike (4) that intrudes the gabbro (Fig. 2). A total of 62 samples were obtained. Results from the gabbro and tonalite only are presented in this paper. Paleomagnetic measurements were performed on a Molspin Minspin magnetometer. Stepwise demagnetization was per- formed on all but one specimen per site using a Schonstedt alternating field (AF) specimen demagnetizer in fields up to 100 mT. The remaining samples were demagnetized using a Schonstedt thermal demagnetization furnace. Three 2.5 cm diameter polished sections per site were examined using high power (X400-1000) oil-immersion reflected-light microscopy. Properties such as crystal form, grain size, primary intergrowths, and alteration products were noted for each polished section. Volume percents of the opaque minerals were estimated by point counting an average of 250 grains per section. Thin sections representative of the Nahant gabbro and tonalite were also examined for evidence of silicate metamorphism. Paleomagnetism and magnetic mineralogy of the Nahant gabbro and tonalite, eastern Massachusetts Department of Geology and Geography, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, MA 01003, U.S.A Received June 25, 1984 Revision accepted April 2, 1985 Paleomagnetic analyses of the Nahant gabbro and an associated tonalite of eastern Massachusetts reveal five separate popu- lations of paleomagnetic directions. The gabbro and tonalite, exposed in the northernmost portion of the Boston Basin, were selected for this study because of the lack of significant macroscopic evidence of penetrative metamorphism or deformation. The tonalite has not been radiometrically dated; however, an Ordovician date has been reported for the gabbro. Detailed petrographic data indicate that the five populations of paleomagnetic directions obtained for the gabbro and tonalite correspond to five styles of magnetic mineral alteration. A mean alteration index was calculated for each site in the Nahant gabbro and tonalite. There is an apparent relationship between magnetite alteration and normalized intensity at a given demagnetization level, with normalized intensity decreasing as magnetite alteration increases. This relationship illustrates the interdependence between paleom

ined. The Nahant gabbro poles are interpreted as representing either a deuteric or a metasomatic chemical remanent magnetization (CRM). The tonalite pole is interpreted as a deuteric CRM. The gabbro and tonalite poles are similar to a number of poles from Ordovician to Devonian intrusives in the Acadia terrane, including the St. Stephen and St. George plutons. Petrographic examination of polished sections from the Devonian St. Stephen and St. George plutons reveals evidence for alteration of primary magnetic mineral assemblages. Similarities exist between these alterations and alterations observed in the Nahant suite, most notably, the formation of titanite from Fe-Ti oxides. The repeated determination of similar poles on intrusive rocks in the Acadia terrane suggests there may be some tectonic or geomagnetic significance to poles from intrusives; however, without more data pertaining to the timing of metasomatic events observed in the Nahant suite and the St. Stephen and St. George plutons, the age and significance of these poles cannot be interpreted with certainty. Its direction, the mean for 12 dykes, incorporating results from 30 paleomagnetic sites, is 115.9", -55.6", yielding a paleomagnetic pole position of latitude 42.7"S, longitude 4.2"E (dm = 7.3", dp = 5.2"). The primary nature of the magnetization can be demonstrated using geochemistry to correlate individual dykes over distances that can exceed 300 km. Whereas the remanence direction varies between dykes, it remains constant along a dyke, sufficient proof that it was formed during initial cooling of the intrusion. Kirschvink's PCA com- puter programme was modified to generate all possible linear segments comprising three or more consecutive points and having a mean angular deviation (MAD) 5 5". Segments chosen to represent remanence components were selected on the basis of lowest MAD value and if their directions were not part of a progressive directional change when compared with those of adjacent and overlapping segments. All components obtained from PCA were checked for validity on vector dia- grams and stereonet plots before final acceptance. Many samples were dominated by a low-coercivity compo- nent, often having a variable direction within a site. Samples showing this behaviour frequently failed to attain stable end points during AF treatment but instead followed remagnetiza- tion circles. The points defining the remagnetization circles were fitted by a least-squares method (Halls 1976) and accepted if the mean radius of the 95% confidence ellipse about the pole (normal to the plane of the circle) was 5 5". The pole data and any stable end points obtained from indepen- dent samples in the same site were then combined to give a site direction using the method of Bailey and Halls (1984). Regional map- ping north of the 52nd parallel (Eade 1966) indicates that minor similar dykes of this trend extend almost to Hudson Bay. The dykes form two chemical suites, one of which is koma- tiitic, the other high-iron tholeiite to tholeiitit andesite. The dykes, however, are parallel and contain a common paleomag- netic component. We later refer to the relationship between tholeiitic and komatiitic dykes of the Molson swarm, which are related to Fox River volcanics of similar age and composition. The evidence favours the idea that the two magma types can be generated essentially simultaneously. We think this is the case with the Mistassini swarm. Most of the samples used in the petrochemical study were collected by E.H.C., D.J., and others during mapping of the Wabissinane River area (Chown and Caty 1972), and chemical analyses of these samples were carried out by D.J. and N.M. at the Geochemistly Laboratoly of the University of Montreal (Table 1). kes extend northwest from the Mistassini embayment and comprise both tholeiitic and komatiitic suites. They are probably > 2000 Ma old and yield two major paleomagnetic components. One of these, with a pole at 131 OW, 13 "S, is thought to be an overprint related to the Elsonian Disturbance 1400- 1500 Ma ago. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: ficance of a swarm of basic dykes that occurs in the Superior Province adjacent to the central Grenville Front. The major concentration of these dykes trends northwest (Fig. 1) from the Mistassini-Otish embayments, so much so as to suggest a genetic relationship between the occurrence of these embayments and intrusion of the dyke swarm. Some of the dykes show up as spectacular linear highs on regional aeromagnetic maps (e.g., Geological Survey of Canada maps 71 12G and 71 15G). Regional map- ping north of the 52nd parallel (Eade 1966) indicates that minor similar dykes of this trend extend almost to Hudson Bay. The dykes form two chemical suites, one of which is koma- tiitic, the other high-iron tholeiite to tholeiitit andesite. The dykes, however, are parallel and contain a common paleomag- netic component. We later refer to the relationship between tholeiitic and komatiitic dykes of the Molson swarm, which are related to Fox River volcanics of similar age and composition. The evidence favours the idea that the two magma types can be generated essentially simultaneously. We think this is the case with the Mistassini swarm. Most of the samples used in the petrochemical study were collected by E.H.C., D.J., and others during mapping of the Wabissinane River area (Chown and Caty 1972), and chemical analyses of these samples were carried out by D.J. and N.M. at the Geochemistly Laboratoly of the University of Montreal (Table 1). We relate the sills, dated at about 0.77 Ga, to the rifting event that led to "Copper cycle" and Rapitan sediments above the MMs, and we suggest that the exposed part of the MMs has an age between 0.88 and 0.77 Ga. The APW path is apparently not affected by rotations: pole evidence indicates little if any relative rotation between thrust sheets of the fold belt or between the fold belt and the craton. Three major poles have been determined from the Katherine Group. The youngest appears to be associated with the Laramide Orogeny . The two older poles, like most others from the Mackenzie Mountains supergroup, lie to the west of older Belt - Purcell poles (Bressler 198 1 ; Elston and McKee 1982). We suggest that one of the Katherine poles is primary; it would therefore be the oldest pole yet determined from the Mackenzie Mountains. The other pole, associated with hematite pigment, helps to document a pervasive magnetization, which is a chemical overprint in units of the Mackenzie Mountains super- group but probably primary in units of the overlying Copper cycle. Present evidence indicates that there has been no rotation of poles, either because of rela- tive rotation between thrust sheets or because of relative rota- tion between the fold belt and the craton, to confuse this interpretation.

(NRM) . Because the derived paleomagnetic poles are undated, it is difficult without other constraints to relate these poles to a given apparent polar wander (APW) path. Three major poles have been determined from the Katherine Group. The youngest appears to be associated with the Laramide Orogeny . The two older poles, like most others from the Mackenzie Mountains supergroup, lie to the west of older Belt - Purcell poles (Bressler 198 1 ; Elston and McKee 1982). We suggest that one of the Katherine poles is primary; it would therefore be the oldest pole yet determined from the Mackenzie Mountains. The other pole, associated with hematite pigment, helps to document a pervasive magnetization, which is a chemical overprint in units of the Mackenzie Mountains super- group but probably primary in units of the overlying Copper cycle. It may record a late Precambrian rifting event. Primary poles from the Katherine, Little Dal, and basic sills appear to document a new segment of the APW path for North America lying west of the Grenville Loop. Present evidence indicates that there has been no rotation of poles, either because of rela- tive rotation between thrust sheets or because of relative rota- tion between the fold belt and the craton, to confuse this interpretation.

It is also possible that flattening of inclination is caused by magnetic anistropy, but tests show this to be unlikely. A third possibility is that the magnetization is secondary and of latest Cretaceous age, but there are good reasons for believing this is not so. Lastly, it is possible that the unit could have been formed close to its present position relative to the craton but was deposited so quickly that the paleosecular variation was not adequately sampled, and the result is only a "spot" reading of the paleofield. The last is our preferred interpretation of the flattened inclination, but the clockwise deflection of the declination could reflect rotation. carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: Volcanogenic sediments of the Fourchu Group and a gabbmic intrusion, which are found in the Avalonian terraile of south- eastern Cape Breton Island, have been sampled for paleomagnetic analysis. Upon detailed thermal and alternating-field demagnetization, three often-superimposed components of magnetization are obtained. One of these is aligned with the present-day geomagnetic field direction in Nova Scotia and is assumed to be of recent origin. The second group of directions is south-southeasterly and shallow, is postfolding in age, and is inferred to represent a Carboniferous overprint. The third direc- tion, carried almost always by hematite, is also postfolding and yields a dual-polarity mean direction to the northwest or south- east, with a Fdirly steep inclination (D = 132", 1 = -63 "). This last direction is not seen in Avalonian or other North American rocks of Devonian or younger age; it is, therefore, bracketed in age between the earliest folding of the rocks and the latest Silurian. Given that Taconic folding has not been reported for this area, we assume that this magnetization was intro- duced in the rocks during uplift and oxidation after an Avalonian folding phase. In addition, subaerial volcanics were sampled at sites 7, 14, and 17. Reddish hematite staining is present in virtually all of these strata to a greater or lesser degree, but the timing of hematite formation could not be assessed from field obsenrations. The gabbro was sampled at Baliene Cove (sites 12 and 18) and at Cape Breton (site 1 1). There are. however, two unresolved questions regarding the history of this area, and paleomagnetic techniques appear to be suitable for eventually providing answers to both. Given that it was not part of North America, did Avalon constitute an independent microplate, or was it attached to another major cratonic block? Well-dated paleo- magnetic results can record the displacements of tectonic ele- ments such as Avalon, through apparent polar wander paths (APWP's) and thus constrain models for the history and orig- inal affinity of the terrane. Laboratory procedure Magnetization (direction and intensity) was measured with a digital Schonstedt spinner magnetometer (DSM- 1) coupled, in tandem, to PDP-11 and Apple I1 minicomputers. Two methods of demagnetization were used. Alternating field (AF) demag- netization was carried out using a solenoid having a maximum intensity of 90 mT, the performance of which was largely improved by adding three large, concentric mu-metal cylinders around the solenoid (Seguin 1975); a three-axis tumbler was used with the unit. Geological setting The roughly 9000 km2 Anticosti Island constitutes the eastern segment of the physiographic region of the St. Lawrence Platform. It lies between the Canadian Shield to the north and the Appalachian Orogen to the south and east. The absence of significant deformational structures in the Anticosti sequence demonstrates that the Anticosti Paleoplatform remained stable through at least two tectonic upheavals: the Taconic and Acadian orogenies. Consequently, old (eventually primary and free from overprints) remanences can be expected on this platform. Stratal deformations attributed to these oro- genic events are mainly restricted to the south of the ancient geosuture called Logan's Line (Poole et ul. 1969). The basal Anticosti stratigraphic sequence rests unconformably on the southeast margin of the Precambrian craton (Richardson 1857). The platform sequence, which forms a wedge from north to south, thickens to in excess of 380 m south of Anti- costi Island. Carbonates, marls , shales, and siliciclastic sands, possibly Cambrian and Early Middle, and in part Late Ordo- vician in age (Twenhofel 1928; Roliff 1968; Riva 1969), occur mainly as sub

Geological setting The roughly 9000 km2 Anticosti Island constitutes the eastern segment of the physiographic region of the St. Lawrence Platform. It lies between the Canadian Shield to the north and the Appalachian Orogen to the south and east. The absence of significant deformational structures in the Anticosti sequence demonstrates that the Anticosti Paleoplatform remained stable through at least two tectonic upheavals: the Taconic and Acadian orogenies. Consequently, old (eventually primary and free from overprints) remanences can be expected on this platform. Stratal deformations attributed to these oro- genic events are mainly restricted to the south of the ancient geosuture called Logan's Line (Poole et ul. 1969). The basal Anticosti stratigraphic sequence rests unconformably on the southeast margin of the Precambrian craton (Richardson 1857). The platform sequence, which forms a wedge from north to south, thickens to in excess of 380 m south of Anti- costi Island. pt-fles layered mafic intrusion is an attractive target for paleomagnetic study because of its Cambrian (540 Ma) age and its suitability for remanence determination due to high magnetite content. Rocks of this age that are undisturbed by Appalachian tectonics are difficult to find in eastern North America. As a result, the paleomagnetic data base from lower Paleozoic rocks from this part of the craton is relatively scanty. Interpretations of the available poles are hampered by a lack of accurate age determinations, by uncertainty about the integrity of the North American craton, and by the possible complexity of the loyer Paleozoic apparent polar wander (APW) path. The Sept-Iles intrusion was studied in order to improve the data base with the intent of eventually establishing a reference APW path for the pre-Appalachian North American craton. This study presents the magnetic history of the gabbroic and anorthositic phases of the intrusion, and some diabase dykes that are possibly related to the same magmatic event. Asitka Group has been described by Lord (1948) and Monger (1977). The most com- plete section lies about 3 krn east of Dewar Peak, in the McConnell Creek map area (56"44'N, 126'49'W). There it forms part of the uplifted rim of upper Paleozoic and lower Mesozoic strata that surrounds the Bowser Basin (BB of Fig. 1). The Early Permian (late Sakrnarian to early Artinskian) age of the Asitka Group is well established (Ross and Monger 1978; Rigby 1973). It was deposited about the middle of the Kiaman superchron, which extends from the Westphalian to the end of the Paleozoic. During the Kiaman, the geomagnetic field was predominantly of reversed polarity. In the Dewar Peak area, the Asitka Group consists of three genemlly southward-dipping units exposed in a faulted succes- sion (Fig. 2). The lowest unit, whose base is faulted against Lower Jurassic rocks of the Hazelton Group to the east, com- prises up to 600 m of basalt, argillite, chert, and carbonate. The middle unit consists of about 1500 m of basalt flows overlain by red flow-banded rhyolite and prophyry with inter- calated breccia. It is unlikely, therefore, that the HT1 magnetization records a reversal of the geomagnetic field that occurred as the lavas initially cooled. As we describe below, the overlying tuffs have directions similar to HT1. One previous result from the Table Head Group on Port au Port Peninsula was reported as an abstract (Evans and Hall 1985) in which, however, there was no mention of the laboratory treatment used. Still unpublished are recent results (Prasad 1986) from the St. George and Table Head groups on the Northern Penin- sula, 170-260 krn north of Port au Port. Geology The rocks we studied form part of the Humber Zone (Williams 1979). According to Williams and Stevens (1974), the lower Paleozoic rocks of this region record the evolution of a platform at the margin of a proto-Atlantic ocean and its partial subduction under oceanic lithosphere. Rodgers and Neale (1963) recognized two distinct sequences in western Newfoundland: autochthonous shallow-water carbonates and minor siliciclastics, and allochthonous deeper water deposits. The general stratigraphy was summarized by Whittington and Kindle (1969). Within the autochthon, Lower Cambrian silici- clastic rocks are overlain by a Middle Cambrian to Lower Orodvician (Port au Port and St. George groups) shall

1979) and other fossil evidence, the age of the Table Head Group is post-Canadian, corresponding to the Whiterock Stage (early Llanvirn, or about 470 -465 Ma). The Cambrian and most of the Ordovician succession on Port au Port Peninsula is gently tilted: dips of the St. George Group and Table Point and Table Cove formations are in the range of 11 - 18"NW to N. Of the three major orogenic events that affected the Humber Zone, the Taconic (mid- to Late Ordovician) orogeny is very unlikely to be a cause of this deformation (O'Brien 1975). Most probably the deformation resulted from the Acadian (Devonian) orogeny (Schillereff and Williams 1979). The effect of the late Paleozoic Alleghenian orogeny in the Humber Zone is minimal compared with its effect elsewhere in the Appalachians (Williams 1980), though a possible Alleghenian deformation in some lower Paleozoic strata in the Humber Zone cannot be excluded (R. Geology The rocks we studied form part of the Humber Zone (Williams 1979). According to Williams and Stevens (1974), the lower Paleozoic rocks of this region record the evolution of a platform at the margin of a proto-Atlantic ocean and its partial subduction under oceanic lithosphere. Rodgers and Neale (1963) recognized two distinct sequences in western Newfoundland: autochthonous shallow-water carbonates and minor siliciclastics, and allochthonous deeper water deposits. The general stratigraphy was summarized by Whittington and Kindle (1969). Within the autochthon, Lower Cambrian silici- clastic rocks are overlain by a Middle Cambrian to Lower Orodvician (Port au Port and St. George groups) shall

1979) and other fossil evidence, the age of the Table Head Group is post-Canadian, corresponding to the Whiterock Stage (early Llanvirn, or about 470 -465 Ma). The Cambrian and most of the Ordovician succession on Port au Port Peninsula is gently tilted: dips of the St. George Group and Table Point and Table Cove formations are in the range of 11 - 18"NW to N. Of the three major orogenic events that affected the Humber Zone, the Taconic (mid- to Late Ordovician) orogeny is very unlikely to be a cause of this deformation (O'Brien 1975). Most probably the deformation resulted from the Acadian (Devonian) orogeny (Schillereff and Williams 1979). The effect of the late Paleozoic Alleghenian orogeny in the Humber Zone is minimal compared with its effect elsewhere in the Appalachians (Williams 1980), though a possible Alleghenian deformation in some lower Paleozoic strata in the Humber Zone cannot be excluded (R. K. Stevens, personal communication, 1986). Sampling and measurement Cambrian and Ordovician formations on Port au Port Penin- sula were sampled in 1982 and 1984 (Prasad 1986). Geology The rocks we studied form part of the Humber Zone (Williams 1979). According to Williams and Stevens (1974), the lower Paleozoic rocks of this region record the evolution of a platform at the margin of a proto-Atlantic ocean and its partial subduction under oceanic lithosphere. Rodgers and Neale (1963) recognized two distinct sequences in western Newfoundland: autochthonous shallow-water carbonates and minor siliciclastics, and allochthonous deeper water deposits. The general stratigraphy was summarized by Whittington and Kindle (1969). Within the autochthon, Lower Cambrian silici- clastic rocks are overlain by a Middle Cambrian to Lower Orodvician (Port au Port and St. George groups) shall

1979) and other fossil evidence, the age of the Table Head Group is post-Canadian, corresponding to the Whiterock Stage (early Llanvirn, or about 470 -465 Ma). The Cambrian and most of the Ordovician succession on Port au Port Peninsula is gently tilted: dips of the St. George Group and Table Point and Table Cove formations are in the range of 11 - 18"NW to N. Of the three major orogenic events that affected the Humber Zone, the Taconic (mid- to Late Ordovician) orogeny is very unlikely to be a cause of this deformation (O'Brien 1975). Most probably the deformation resulted from the Acadian (Devonian) orogeny (Schillereff and Williams 1979). The effect of the late Paleozoic Alleghenian orogeny in the Humber Zone is minimal compared with its effect elsewhere in the Appalachians (Williams 1980), though a possible Alleghenian deformation in some lower Paleozoic strata in the Humber Zone cannot be excluded (R. K. Stevens, personal communication, 1986). Sampling and measurement Cambrian and Ordovician formations on Port au Port Penin- sula were sampled in 1982 and 1984 (Prasad 1986). Furthermore, the problem is exacer- bated by the structural complexities of the region and by the fact that because the paleolatitude is high the inclinations are steep and paleolatitude is difficult to determine. In the area sampled, volcanic rocks of the Isachsen Forma- tion range in age from Barremian to Aptian. During this time interval the youngest of the M sequence of reversals of the geomagnetic field occurred. These reversals have been docu- mented in carbonate sections in Italy (Lowrie et al. 1980), but carbonates are not amenable to isotopic dating, whereas the Isachsen basalts are. Our second objective, therefore, was to identify horizons of reversed magnetization corresponding to these anomalies in rocks that could be both paleontologically and isotopically dated. This would refine the reversal time scale and expedite its correlation to the biostratigraphic time scale for the Early Cretaceous, a key interval of time. Earth Sci. 25, 1407-1419 (1988) Introduction The early Paleozoic sedimentary rocks of the Port au Port Peninsula of western Newfoundland were deposited on the margin of cratonal North America facing the lapetus ocean (Cocks and Fortey 1982). These rocks were subsequently deformed during the middle to Late Ordovician Taconic and the Devonian Acadian orogenic events. All of these sequences today fall within the Humber Zone of the Appalachian orogen (Williams 1978). Paleomagnetic analysis of Ordovician rocks on the Port au Port Peninsula was undertaken to determine the effects of the deformation of this continental margin particularly as they may be reflected by tectonic rotation, and also to characterize the nature of the Earth's magnetic field during part of the Ordovician. Both of these goals can be met only if the acquisi- tion of remanence can be shown to be primary, or at least very early in the history of these rocks. As the age of some of the units sampled in this study, for example the Llanvirnian Table Head Group, is very close to the age of the earliest deforma- tion, there

. The rocks sampled in this study range in age from Tremado- cian - Arenigian (St. George Group) to Llandeilian - Carado- cian (Lourdes Limestone), but the principal focus of this study lies with the stratigraphically well-defined Table Head Group, which is Llanvirnian in age. The results from the units older and younger than the Table Head Group are of a preliminary nature and a more comprehensive analysis of these results will be incorporated in a subsequent paper dealing with the greater western Newfoundland area. In this setting, packages of rocks have been identified in western Newfoundland largely on the basis of whether they form part of the autochthon (remnants of the early Paleozoic continental margin) or the allochthon (remnants of the large-scale thrust sheets associated with the obduction event). These packages are subsequently deformed during the mid-Paleozoic Acadian orogeny (Williams and Hatcher 1983). The Port au Port Peninsula sits within the Humber Zone of western Newfoundland and has been the subject of geologic investigations since the last century (see Schuchert and Dunbar 1934 for a historical perspective of Newfoundland geology). The Peninsula is characterized by extensive outcrops of Cam- brian and Ordovician sequences that have been interpreted to represent part of the autochthonous stable continental margin sequence. VOL. 25, 1988 Summary and conclusions A paleomagnetic study of the Llanvirnian Table Head Group in the Port au Port region of western Newfoundland indicates that the rocks have a relatively simple two-component magne- tization history comprising a low-temperature, low-coercivity present field overprint, and a stable, southeasterly magnetiza- tion with a shallow to moderate inclination acquired during a reverse polarity of the Earth's field. Results Alaska Peninsula Geologic Setting of the Jurassic of the Alaska Peninsula The best geologic summary of the Alaska Peninsula available to date is that of Burk ( 1965). Basically, volcanic-rich rock units of early Jurassic age conformably overlie late Triassic rocks. Along the southern coast of the Alaska Peninsula the fossiliferous early Juras- sic sediments consist of tuffaceous sandstone, calcareous sandstone and shale, limestone, and volcanic conglo~erate grading upward to fine- grained shale and sandstone. Inland, early Jurassic porphyritic flows, breccia, and tuff make up much of the section. A very complete section of middle and late Jurassic sedimentary rocks is well-exposed in the Tuxedni Bay region, and conformably overlies the early Jurassic. Part of this section, the Tuxedni group, is composed of siltstone, arkose, graywacke, sandstone, conglomerate, massive sandstone, and shale (Detterman and Hartsock 1966). Abstract The remanent magnetization of the andesitic cover of the Sesia-Lanzo Zone has been studied from 16 sites along three transversal sections. The remanent magnetization of the rock is stable and it appears to be primary after a conglomerate test. The mean direction of magnetization is consistent for all sites, but for one exception, with satisfactory values of statistiea] parameters. Therefore no deformation structures postdating the acquisition of remanent magnetization can be inferred from palaeomagnetic data. The mean direction of magnetization (11 sites, 152 specimens) is: D = 185.9, I = ~2.9, with a95 = 8.8. No tec- tonic correction can yet be made. estudying the paleomag- netism of the Wigwam Formation. Geological setting Our study area (Fig. 1) lies in the middle of the Botwood Group, which extends over 200 km southwest from Change Islands. Near its type area around the Bay of Exploits, the Botwood Group consists of subaerial mafic and felsic volcanic rocks of the Lawrenceton Formation conformably overlain by the redbeds and minor volcanics of the Wigwam Formation. Our paleomagnetic sites are all in the Wigwam Formation (Fig. 2). Near the south end of the Bay of Exploits, the Wigwam Formation contains limestone beds that bear late Llandovery to early Wenlock fossils (Williams 1972). Identification of a Wenlock to early Ludlow Monograptus near Glenwood is now suspect (Elliot et al. 1991). On Change Islands, the Lawrence- ton Formation contains early and late Llandovery fossils (van der Pluijm et al. 1987), suggesting that the Wigwam Formation is not older than Llandovery. On the Port Albert Peninsula (southwest of Change Islands), the Wigwam Formation is intruded by dykes yielding a 422 + 3 Ma U-Pb zircon age (Elliot et al. 1991). The Wigwam Formation appears to be overlain by Stony Lake volcanic rocks which yield a U-Pb zircon date of 423'; Ma (Dunning et al. 1990). Both of these U-Pb ages suggest that
