carrier_identity_candidates.excerpt: Formation data rules out the pos- sibility that a significant partial overprint has affected the primary remanence in these rocks. Starkey and Palmer (1970) have pointed out that a small partial overprint superimposed along a consistent direction upon a random scatter of predepo- sitional remanence directions in conglomerate clasts is not readily detected by the randomness test. However, a partial overprint should result in systematic directional swings as individual conglomerate clasts are demagnetized since block- ing temperature spectra for the two magnetizations are unlikely to be identical (especially in clasts containing both magnetite and hematite, as at site 18). Also, a partial overprint should cause asymmetry in the reversal pattern observed between stably magnetized sites. A partial overprint in rocks of the Wigwam Formation seems unlikely because almost all speci- mens at sites 18 and 35 carry stable directions of magnetiza- tion, and mean directions for sites magnetized to the north and south are antiparallel within the limits of statistical uncer- tainty. Paleomagnetic investigations of the Emsian quartz sandstones from Holy Cross Mountains (Central Poland) have revealed the presence of a three-component natural remanent magnetization. The viscous component of the NRM is carried by magnetite grains and is directed close to the present-day local geomagnetic field. The remaining two components are both carried by hematite, presumably of two-stage origin. Because it was not possible to apply a fold test, the acquisition time of each component could only be inferred indirectly. The hematite remanence of the highest (65OOC) blocking temperature is thought to be of post-tectonic (Permian) origin, as its direction before bedding correction (D = 199 ‘, Z = - 38” ) is almost identical with the characteristic NRM obtained (Lewandowski, 1983) from neighbouring Permian deposits. The intermediate component (D = 231°, Z = 0, with a blocking temperature of around 610°C), after applying a bedding correction, gives a paleomagnetic pole (h = 24ON, S$ = 142OE) near to European Middle-Upper Devonian poles. Therefore, it is thought that this magnetization probably reflects the ambient geomagnetic field not very long after sedimentation. Introduction During the past few years, intensive pale

Introduction During the past few years, intensive paleo- magnetic studies of the Devonian rocks have been made both from the European continent (Abra- hamsen, 1977; Duff, 1980; Bachtadse et al., 1983; Perroud and Bonhommet, 1984) and the British Isles (Storetvedt and Carmichael, 1979; Storetvedt and Torsvik, 1983; Torsvik et al., 1983; Torsvik, 1984, 1985). Although unequivocal geotectonic in- terpretation of the results obtained so far is not possible, nonetheless some general conclusions have been drawn concerning geodynamic processes during the assembly of Pangea (e.g. Van der Voo, 1983). This paper reports paleomagnetic results from the Holy Cross Mountains (Central Poland). The investigation is part of the research program on the Upper Palaeozoic rocks from Norway (in- cluding Spitsbergen) and Poland, carried out by paleomagnetic groups in Bergen and Sogndal (Norway) and Warsaw (Poland). The Spitsbergen results have already been published (Lovlie et al., 1984; Jelehska and Lewandowski, in press). w poorly dated palaeomagnetic directions are reported from Africa, the other large plate inferred to have played an important role in the tectonic development of the Mediterranean region. In contrast to the major plates, the main sources of palaeomagnetic data in the Mediterranean have been Mesozoic and Palaeogene carbonates, precluding direct compari- son between directions measured from the Medi- terranean and the European and African plates. Thus, for a lack of a better solution, Mediter- ranean palaeopoles are usually compared with poles for Africa or Europe with the help of a plate tectonic reconstruction (VandenBerg, 1979, Lowrie et al., 1980, Marton and Marton, 1981, 1983). This procedure allows common trends or large relative movements in the Mediterranean to be recognized with respect to the major plates. However, there are shortcomings to the use of the “pseudo” ap- parent polar wander path (APWP) and work con- tinues to be directed in the stable areas at develop- ing better defined APWPs. Until additional results are reported from the stable areas, studies in structurally rotated terranes are best continued in strata the directions of which can be directly com- pared with those already reported from the major plates. w poorly dated palaeomagnetic directions are reported from Africa, the other large plate inferred to have played an important role in the tectonic development of the Mediterranean region. In contrast to the major plates, the main sources of palaeomagnetic data in the Mediterranean have been Mesozoic and Palaeogene carbonates, precluding direct compari- son between directions measured from the Medi- terranean and the European and African plates. Thus, for a lack of a better solution, Mediter- ranean palaeopoles are usually compared with poles for Africa or Europe with the help of a plate tectonic reconstruction (VandenBerg, 1979, Lowrie et al., 1980, Marton and Marton, 1981, 1983). However, there are shortcomings to the use of the “pseudo” ap- parent polar wander path (APWP) and work con- tinues to be directed in the stable areas at develop- ing better defined APWPs. Discussion The complex NRM at locality 6 (Table 1) serves as a base for evaluating the timing of acquisition of the remanence of red beds from the Balaton Highlands. The component 6a direction is consid- ered to be a primary remanence, although not necessarily of depositional origin for several rea- sons. It resides in haematite that is extremely resistant to thermal cleaning; the structurally un- corrected direction differs significantly from the present field direction, and the tilt-corrected in- clination is low enough to be a Permian inclina- tion. Additionally, the polarity may be concluded to be reverse by correlation with the already proven post-Permian counterclockwise rotation of the Transdanubian Central Mountains (e.g. Marton and Marton, 1983). Lastly, the declination after tilt correction agrees with some other directions interpreted as Permian from the eastern part of the Southern and Eastern Alps and the Inner West Carpathians (Fig. 7). 49 The overprint component at locality 6 (Table 1, direction 6b), although resistant to heating and differing significantly from the present field direc- tion, is less resistant to thermal cleaning than direction 6a. It shows a remarkable similarity to di

ions, and agreement of the struc- turally uncorrected ChRM direction of locality 1 with the secondary directions may be a coinci- dence. In any case, a general interpretation of palaeo- magnetic results from the Balaton Highlands in terms of tectonics is basically independent of the correct answer to the above question. With respect to stable Europe, represented by the Bohemian Massif in the present vicinity of the Pannonian Basin, a large counterclockwise rotation of the Balaton Highlands is evident. The amount of rota- tion exceeds 90” for the direction interpreted as Permian, and appears distinctly less for the over- printed normal polarity directions.
